## Overview

```{=html}
<div class="case-intro-grid">
  <div class="case-intro-card">

      This project evaluates downside risk for a diversified portfolio and compares

    </p>
```

The sample contains daily adjusted market prices from 2015 through the end of
2025. The portfolio combines equities, bonds and gold to create a simple
multi-asset allocation suitable for illustrating portfolio-level downside risk.

## Methodology

```{=html}
<div class="method-grid">
  <div class="method-card">
    <span>01</span>
    <h3>Market Data</h3>
    <p>Collect adjusted daily prices for SPY, IEF and GLD.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="method-card">
    <span>02</span>
    <h3>Portfolio Returns</h3>
    <p>Convert prices to log returns and aggregate them using fixed portfolio weights.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="method-card">
    <span>03</span>
    <h3>Historical Risk</h3>
    <p>Estimate 99% Value at Risk and Conditional Value at Risk from realized returns.</p>
  </div>

  <div class="method-card">
    <span>04</span>
    <h3>Monte Carlo</h3>
    <p>Generate 10,000 daily return scenarios from the historical mean and volatility.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

Daily log returns are calculated as

$$
r_t = \ln\left(\frac{P_t}{P_{t-1}}\right).
$$

Historical VaR identifies the loss threshold exceeded by roughly the worst 1% of
observations. CVaR measures the average loss beyond that threshold.

```{=html}
<div class="result-grid">

  <div class="result-card featured-result">

    <span class="result-label">MONTE CARLO VaR</span>

  </div>

  <div class="result-card">
    <span class="result-label">MONTE CARLO CVaR</span>
    <strong>1.60%</strong>
    <small>99% expected shortfall</small>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="case-insight">
  <span class="case-label">MAIN TAKEAWAY</span>
  <p>
    Historical tail losses are larger than those produced by the normal Monte
    Carlo baseline. The gap is most visible in CVaR:
    <strong>2.52%</strong> historically versus <strong>1.60%</strong> in simulation.
  </p>
</div>
```

The portfolio produced an annualized historical return of approximately
**9.01%** with annualized volatility of **9.64%**. The largest daily loss in the
sample was approximately **5.83%**.

## Analysis

### Relative asset performance

Normalizing each asset series to 100 provides a common starting point and makes
the different long-run paths of equities, bonds and gold easier to compare.
In practical terms, SPY is the growth engine, IEF acts as the stabilizer, and
GLD provides diversification against equity stress.

```{=html}
<div class="analysis-note">
  <span class="analysis-icon">↗</span>
  <div>
    <strong>Interpretation</strong>
    <p>Comparing normalized price paths highlights how each sleeve contributes differently to return generation and diversification.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

### Historical versus simulated downside risk

The simulated normal baseline produces smaller 99% tail-risk estimates than the
historical return distribution. This indicates that the simple parametric
simulation understates the severity of downside outcomes observed in the sample.

```{=html}
<div class="analysis-note">
  <span class="analysis-icon">!</span>
  <div>
    <strong>Interpretation</strong>
    <p>Historical downside risk remains the more conservative benchmark for this portfolio under severe conditions.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

### Monte Carlo return distribution

The simulated distribution is useful as a baseline, but it produces a thinner
left tail than the historical data. This is why the Monte Carlo VaR and CVaR
figures remain below the empirical historical estimates.

```{=html}
<div class="analysis-note">
  <span class="analysis-icon">∿</span>
  <div>
    <strong>Interpretation</strong>
    <p>The gap between simulated and historical tail losses suggests non-normal features such as fat tails in realized returns.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

### Historical stress episodes

Historical portfolio returns reveal periods of unusually large gains and losses.
Large negative observations tend to cluster around market stress regimes rather
than appearing as isolated random events.

```{=html}
<div class="analysis-note">
  <span class="analysis-icon">—</span>
  <div>
    <strong>Interpretation</strong>
    <p>Stress episodes are not evenly distributed over time, which supports extending the model with time-varying volatility in future work.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

## Conclusion

The project demonstrates a transparent workflow for moving from market prices to
portfolio returns, historical tail-risk estimation and Monte Carlo stress
testing.

The key comparison is between **realized historical losses** and a
**normal-distribution simulation baseline**. Historical VaR and especially
historical CVaR are larger, indicating that the simple parametric model does not
fully reproduce the severity of downside observations present in the historical
sample.

A natural next step would be to extend the framework with fat-tailed
distributions, time-varying volatility, dynamic correlations, multi-day risk
horizons and explicit historical crisis scenarios.
